sections.text: O Arjuna! There is nothing higher than Me; all is strung upon Me as rows of pearls upon a thread.
O Arjuna! I am the Fluidity in water, the Light in the sun and in the moon. I am the mystic syllable Om in the Vedic scriptures, the Sound in ether, the Virility in man.
पुण्यो गन्धः पृथिव्यां च तेजश्चास्मि विभावसौ।
I am the Fragrance of earth, the Brilliance of fire. I am the Life Force in all beings, and I am the Austerity of the ascetics.

We have been discussing Chapter 7, Gnana Vignana Yoga, the Yoga of Knowledge and Wisdom. In the beginning, Bhagavan said, Im going to tell you who I am, and Ill tell you all about it without leaving anything behind. And then he basically said that what you see in this world is my Eightfold Prakriti.
We all claim that we have never seen Bhagavan before. We have never seen God. We have never known Him. Bhagawan says, You know me every day, you meet me every day. You just dont recognize it. Because what you see is the Bhoomi, Apaha, Analaha, Kham, Vayuhu -- the five elements which make up the entire world of ours. It is nothing but my own manifestation.
Then he also included Manas, Buddhi, Ahankara. When we think about the five elements, we only think about the insentient world, the world of matter. We say, Well, we are human beings, we are living beings. But no -- even my mind, my intellect, my ego. Bhagavan said, thats my Prakriti.
Thats my own nature, you know, its my own manifestation. So when you include all of that, that includes all the beings and things, theres nothing left behind. He said, thats nothing but me manifesting in my Eightfold Prakriti. You know me -- you just are not capable of grasping the totality of His expression. With that, he progressed and said, Well then, let me explain to you that all these beings have come out of me. I am the source of all beings and I am the resting place for all beings.
There is nothing other than Him in this world, but in His manifestation as the Eightfold Prakriti, I dont see Him in His totality. So he proceeds further in verse seven to say how everything is connected. Right now we dont feel connected to anything. No matter how hard we try, we feel like I am an island in this universe.
By myself, I am so unique. Everything else is the world. All beings are part of the world. Thats what we call Jagat. We complain in Hindi all the time, you know, Jagat. Because we consider ourselves to be so unique, we are not part of this Jagat.
We are not part of this world. Even though our intellect says I am part of this world, our heart doesnt agree. We feel outside of it. We are in the center of our own universe. When I see the world this way, I dont see connection.
How am I connected to the rest of the world? Verse 7 says: Mattah parataram na anyat kinchit asti dhananjaya. There is nothing that exists other than me. So how can you exist without me? From that one singularity, the whole plurality came out. Everything in the plurality is part of that.
If I am part of this world, I am part of that singularity. Therefore there is nothing other than me exist. You are no other than my own self. He said, I am the common thread. The expression in English is thats the common thread -- the common thread in all these things and beings which keeps them together as the world.
The Self is the common thread. Even though right now I think myself is completely different than yourself and herself and himself -- that self remains constant in all beings. I am that common thread which keeps this universe together. The analogy, obviously, is sutre manigana iva -- in the pearl necklace, beads are all separate from each other.
But the thread keeps them together as a necklace. So I am that common thread. What is common in me and you? You also call it myself when you express yourself. That self, Bhagavan said, is the common thread among all beings. And then, obviously, for people like us who cant really understand without elaborate examples --
We can only relate to something when somebody gives an example about something we know. This may still remain abstract, but then he says, Okay, let me explain to you how it works. So the next verse says: Raso aham apsu kaunteya prabhasmi shashisuryayoh pranavah sarva vedeshu shabdah khe purusham nrshu. In other words, Now let me enumerate things you can understand. I am the liquidity in water. I am the radiance in moon and sun.
Whatever we think is the unique quality of that thing or being -- he said, thats because of me. Because I reside in that being or thing, it makes the thing what it is. What is dharma in Sanskrit? That which holds is dharma. As I always use the example: the dharma of sugar is sweetness. As long as it is sweet, it is sugar. It may look like sugar, it may feel like sugar, but if it doesnt taste like sugar, its not sugar.
So the dharma of a thing or being -- what makes it what it is -- Bhagavan says that dharma is me. Because of that dharma, things and beings are what they are. Then he continues in the next verses: Punyo gandhah prithivyam cha tejash chasmi vibhavasau jivanam sarvabhuteshu tapash chasmi tapasvisu. I am the sweet fragrance of this earth. Im the radiance in fire, and Im the life in all beings.
Very clearly he says, I am the life in all beings. Tapash chasmi tapasvisu. In other words, anything which makes anybody what it is, is me. Living beings are living because of my presence in them. Its a profound statement which we all basically know. We have accepted: Bijam mam sarvabhutanam viddhi partha sanatanam.
Know that I am the source of all beings. I am the seed of all beings. The beings cannot exist without me. Buddhir buddhimatam asmi. I am the intellect in the intellectual, the brilliance in the brilliant.
So if I think that I am so smart, my ego says, Its because of my intellect. Bhagavan says, Mr. Ego, you have really nothing to do with it. I am the intellect in the intellectual, and I am the brilliance in the brilliant. And obviously, Balam Balavatam asmi Kama Raga Vivarjitam. Here is a very interesting point he makes: I am the strength in the strong.
I am the power in the powerful. But Kama Raga Vivarjitam -- that strength is devoid of desire or attachment. It is strength without any association with desire. We only desire strength if we can use it. Isnt there an expression: What is the use of power if I cant abuse it? So this is power without any desire to abuse it.
Thats what we would call sattvic strength. So Bhagavan said, I am the strength in the strong. But when the strong misuse that strength and hurt others, thats not me. So this is like, you know, He very conveniently keeps out of all the trouble we get into. Hey Bhagavan, if youre giving this guy all this mighty power, hell want to hurt us! Bhagavan says, I am the strength in him.
But I am not the one who is hurting you. Dharma Aviruddha, Bhuteshu Kamo Asmi Bharatarshapa. Now I say, okay, what happens to all these desires we have? He said, thats also me. But that is Dharma Aviruddha. We have always this argument.
Is the desire good or bad? You know, Vedantic discussion. We say, yeah, but thats also our desire. I said, well, I want to do good thing. Well, thats also desire. Well, I want to meet Bhagavan.
So if you see in our tradition, when Brahmacharis go to the guru, they first shave all their hair off. That basically indicates getting rid of all desires. Youre a student now, youre a seeker. You shouldnt have any other desire. But they leave a Choti -- that indicates the Shastra Vasana, the desire for knowledge.
That Choti keeps him tied to the Sastra. Then when he becomes a Sanyasi, when that Choti is gone, when you reach a level, even attachment to the Sastra should be dropped. Because otherwise I just remain a pure Pandit. Thats an attachment. Its a golden chain, Bhagawan. So even that has to be dropped.
So when he becomes a Sanyasi -- Sanyasi literally means one who has renounced -- he has renounced everything, all attachment. The Choti goes away. Even Shastra Vasana is not there. That too becomes bondage, so even that needs to go.
So where do these desires stand? Bhagwan said, Desires are nothing but me. I am expressing through you as your desire. But that is Dharma Aviruddha -- not contrary to your Dharma. When you have a desire in accordance with your Dharma, that is legitimate. I am a doctor and I have a desire to help people, perform surgery, or practice my art of medicine. Thats a Dharma-aligned desire.
Thats not a desire which is wrong. Bhagavan said, I am the desire in you which is in line with your Dharma. If Im a father and I want to take care of my children, thats in line with my Dharma. If Im a teacher and I want to make sure my students learn, thats a desire in line with my Dharma. If I am a postman and I want to deliver mail, thats in line with my Dharma. Where we get confused in our understanding of Vedanta is this: Vedanta doesnt say desire is something outside of this world.
We dont import it from somewhere. Its part of your nature, part of Bhagavans nature. But it has to align with your Dharma, without any contradiction. Im a treasurer in a bank, but I want to become the owner of the bank by dealing under the table? Thats obviously contrary to my position. So Bhagawan says, I am the strength in the strong, but without any attachment or desire to use this strength in a manner contrary to Dharma.
Therefore, Bhagavan Bhagavad Gita asks Arjuna to fight. Well, is it right or wrong? Bhagavad says, it is in line with your Dharma. You are the general of this army. All these people are relying on you. You have to use your strength to fight your battle.
So the very important point is: desires are natural as long as they are in line with your duties. I want to take care of my children -- thats in line with my Dharma. Ye chaiva Sattvika Bhava Rajasas Tamasash cha ye. Whatever beings are Sattvic, Rajasic, or Tamasic -- we classify people and things into these categories by their own nature. We know, or at least we have learned from the Upanishads and Bhagavad Gita, that this world is made up of these three Gunas: Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas.
Everything else we see is the permutation and combination of these three gunas. When I have four-color printing, I may have hundreds of colors on my picture, but they are nothing but the permutation and combination of the four colors. Therefore my printer will say yellow is out, and I replace the yellow.

There is nothing higher than Me; all is strung upon Me as rows of pearls upon a thread. This image of the pearl necklace offers a powerful contemplation for today. We see individual beads and think they are separate, but an invisible thread holds them together as one necklace. What is the common thread connecting you to your family, your colleagues, even strangers you pass on the street? Krishna says it is the Self, the I am that each being experiences. Today, when someone speaks to you, try to sense that same thread of consciousness animating both of you.
Krishna then gives specific examples: I am the fluidity in water, the light in sun and moon, the sacred syllable Om, the sound in ether, the virility in man, the fragrance of earth, the brilliance in fire, the life in all beings. These verses teach us to see the Divine not in abstract theology but in immediate experience. What makes water, water? Its wetness, its fluidity. What makes fire, fire? Its heat and brilliance. That essential quality, that dharma, which makes each thing what it is, is the Divine presence.
Today, practice this recognition exercise: For each element you encounter, ask What is its essential quality? and recognize that quality as a direct expression of the Divine. The sweetness in your morning fruit, the warmth of sunlight on your skin, the stability of the ground beneath your feet. Can you move through an entire day holding this awareness?
